response.query: Which objective measures (saliva cotinine, immunization registry linkage, wrist accelerometer) are feasible in an N≈80–120 pilot and what uptake/attrition impacts are realistic?
response.answer: Saliva cotinine, immunization registry linkage, and wrist accelerometer are feasible in an N≈80–120 pilot. Realistic uptake is high, and attrition is low. Feasibility and compliance are well-documented.

results.title: Immunization registry - Wikipedia
results.content: An **immunization registry** or **immunization information system** (**IIS**) is an information system that collects vaccination data about all persons within a geographic area. Immunization information systems (IIS) are an important tool to increase and sustain high vaccination coverage") by consolidating vaccination records of children and adults from multiple providers, forecasting next doses past due, due, and next due to support generating reminder and recall vaccination notices for each individual, and providing official vaccination forms and vaccination coverage assessments. One of the national health objectives "Objective (goal)") is to increase to 95% the proportion of children aged <6 years who participate in fully operational population-based IIS.*[citation needed*]. A "fully operational" IIS includes 95% enrollment or higher of all catchment area "Catchment area (human geography)") children less than 6 years of age with 2 or more immunization encounters administered according to ACIP recommendations.*[citation needed*]. In a population-based IIS, children are entered into the IIS at birth, often through a linkage with electronic birth records. An IIS record also can be initiated by a health care provider at the time of a child's first immunization. If an IIS includes all children in a given geographical area and all providers are reporting immunization information, it can provide a single data source for all community immunization partners. Such a population-based IIS can make it easier to carry out the demonstrably effective immunization strategies (e.g., reminder/recall, AFIX"), and WIC linkages) and thereby decrease the resources needed to achieve and maintain high levels of coverage. IIS can also be used to enhance adult immunization") services and coverage. Pharmacy immunizations are reported to state IIS, allowing for a complete lifetime immunization history.*[citation needed*]. Records of these immunizations often are based on computerized information systems designed for other purposes, such as billing. Although an IIS includes all immunizations administered by health care providers participating in it, only population-based IIS are capable of providing information on all children and all adult doses of vaccines administered by all providers.*[citation needed*]. * Articles needing additional references from February 2016. * All articles needing additional references. * All articles with unsourced statements. * Articles with unsourced statements from September 2022.

results.title: What Is Cotinine and Why Is It Measured? - Biology Insights
results.content: # What Is Cotinine and Why Is It Measured? Cotinine is a chemical compound formed when nicotine is processed in the body. It serves as a reliable marker for detecting nicotine exposure, primarily from tobacco products. Its presence indicates nicotine absorption, whether through active use or environmental exposure, making it a key tool for monitoring intake. Cotinine is the main metabolite of nicotine, formed when nicotine breaks down in the body. Approximately 70-80% of absorbed nicotine transforms into cotinine. Cotinine is a significant biomarker due to its stability and longer presence compared to nicotine. Nicotine has a short half-life (2-3 hours), making extended exposure detection difficult. Cotinine, however, has a significantly longer half-life (12-20 hours), allowing detection for several days. This extended window makes it a practical indicator for assessing recent nicotine use from tobacco products and nicotine replacement therapies. ## How Cotinine is Measured. Cotinine can be measured in various biological samples: urine, blood (serum or plasma), saliva, and hair. Laboratory methods for cotinine detection include immunoassays and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). These techniques allow accurate assessment of cotinine levels across sample types. ## Understanding Cotinine Test Results. Cotinine test results are interpreted by understanding what different concentration ranges indicate about nicotine exposure. Undetectable or very low levels (typically below 1 ng/mL in serum) suggest no recent nicotine exposure, characteristic of non-smokers. For active users of tobacco or nicotine products, cotinine levels are significantly higher. Average cotinine levels for adult smokers in the U.S. can exceed 100 ng/mL, with heavy smokers reaching much higher concentrations. ## Factors Affecting Cotinine Levels. Several factors can influence an individual’s cotinine levels, even with similar nicotine exposure. Individuals with genetic variations leading to reduced CYP2A6 activity may metabolize nicotine more slowly, resulting in higher, longer-persisting cotinine levels. The health of an individual’s liver and kidneys also influences cotinine levels. The liver is where most nicotine metabolism occurs, so its health impacts cotinine conversion. The kidneys eliminate cotinine; impaired function can lead to higher concentrations due to slower excretion. External factors, such as nicotine product type and amount, exposure duration, and certain medications, can also affect cotinine metabolism and overall levels.

results.title: Development and feasibility of a wearable infant wrist band for the objective measurement of physical activity using accelerometery | Pilot and Feasibility Studies | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Development and feasibility of a wearable infant wrist band for the objective measurement of physical activity using accelerometery | Pilot and Feasibility Studies | Springer Nature Link
The following criteria will be used to determine feasibility and acceptability: (1) the majority of participants (> 80%) should wear the band for at least three, but up to seven, days consecutively; (2) the majority of data produced (> 80%) should be technically reliable; (3) the band should fit an Axivity AX3 accelerometer; (4) the band should be worn for the required number of days by the majority (> 80%) of infants and toddlers between the ages of 3–24 months; and (5) the majority of mothers (> 80%) should rate the acceptability of the device as high according to the design specifications—comfort (very comfortable or comfortable), safety (very happy or happy), the buttoning mechanism (easy to unbutton), and drying capability (very quickly or quickly). The aims of this study were to report on the development of an infant wearable band and to examine the feasibility (technical reliability and compliance of the data obtained) and acceptability of this band for the observational measurement of physical activity using accelerometers in infants. The infant wearable band was considered to be feasible and acceptable in this context based on a priori criteria stated in the introduction: (1) the majority of participants (> 95%) wore the band for at least three, but up to seven, days consecutively; (2) the majority of data produced was technically reliable (99% correctly initialised and 100% correctly downloaded); (3) the band was able to fit an Axivity AX3 accelerometer; (4) the band was worn for the required number of days by the majority of infants and toddlers of various ages (91% of 3-month infants, 100% of 6-month infants, 100% of 12-month toddlers, 90% of 18-month toddlers and 88% of 24-month toddlers); and (5) the majority of mothers (80–95%) rated the acceptability of the device as high according to the design specifications—comfort (90%), safety (87%), buttoning mechanism (95%) and drying capability (80%). The infant wrist-worn wearable band housing an appropriate accelerometer is thus recommended for future observational measurement of infant and toddler physical activity, in order to provide comparable, objective data, while maintaining safety and acceptability standards as communicated by mothers.
